title: Machine learning identifies a projected shift from DIC- to alkalinity-dominated ocean CO₂-flux variability
summary: Kernel ridge regression reconstructed present and future air–sea CO₂-flux variability in five Earth-system models. The analysis found dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and alkalinity to be the main drivers, while DIC’s relative importance generally declines in warming scenarios—especially in the equatorial Pacific, Southern Ocean and North Atlantic—as anthropogenic carbon uptake flattens vertical DIC gradients. This result is conditional on the models and scenarios analyzed.
ai_technology: Kernel ridge regression and machine-learning clustering/classification
organization: NORCE Norwegian Research Centre; Bjerknes Centre for Climate Research

evidence.tested: Kernel ridge regression reconstructed present and future air–sea CO₂-flux variability in five Earth-system models.
evidence.unknown: This is an analysis of outputs from five Earth-system models and four historical/future scenarios, not a measurement of future ocean conditions. The interpretation that anthropogenic-carbon-driven gradient flattening contributes to reduced DIC importance is the authors’ proposed mechanism; relative predictor importance does not alone establish causal attribution.
evidence.ai_role: Kernel ridge regression reconstructed CO₂-flux variability from Earth-system-model variables; machine-learning analysis compared predictor importance among spatial clusters and climate scenarios to identify the changing roles of DIC and alkalinity.
